stem: Which of the following best explains how the policy in this address differed from the foreign policy the United States followed for most of the 1920s?

options.text: The United States accepted the League of Nations as the center of its foreign policy.
options.misconception: America stayed out of the League of Nations after World War I; the Truman Doctrine did not change that.

options.text: The United States signed a treaty promising never to use its armed forces outside the Americas.
options.misconception: The 1920s pattern was avoiding alliances and commitments, not a treaty banning force outside the Americas.

options.text: The United States returned to the high tariffs and immigration limits of the 1920s.
options.misconception: High tariffs and immigration limits were 1920s domestic policies, not the foreign policy Truman was changing.

options.text: The United States accepted lasting responsibility for the security of other nations against communism.

rationales.A: The United States never joined the League of Nations, in the 1920s or in 1947. Truman worked through American aid, not through the League.
rationales.B: No such treaty existed. The United States had fought in Europe in both world wars; the 1920s habit was avoiding lasting commitments, not a promise never to fight.
rationales.C: Tariffs and immigration limits were domestic policies of the 1920s. They have nothing to do with Truman's promise of foreign aid.
rationales.D: The address pledged American support to free peoples resisting communist pressure, beginning with Greece and Turkey. Background: that pledge made the United States a permanent guardian of non-communist states, the opposite of the distance it kept in the 1920s.
rationales.general:
1. Recall the 1920s. Background from the books: after World War I, the United States refused to join the League of Nations and kept its distance from Europe's quarrels.
2. Read Truman's ask. Aid to Greece and Turkey, and a promise to support free peoples facing communist pressure.
3. Compare the two. The 1920s said Europe's troubles were not America's business. Truman said they were.
4. Name the change. America moved from keeping its distance to accepting a lasting role as the defender of non-communist states.
Remember: the Truman Doctrine ended the idea that the United States could stay out of the world's struggles.
